title: How the App Connector runbook checks high CPU, memory and disk utilization: process checks, thresholds, local memory endpoints and cleanup
aliases: Managing high CPU, memory, and disk utilization concerns

prose.label: CPU.
prose.text: {{cpu-process-check}} {{cpu-multicore}} {{cpu-support-threshold}} {{gap:memory-threshold}} The group-level CPU headroom limit is in [[zpa.app-connectors.performance]].

cpu-process-check.statement: For high CPU the runbook uses ps aux --sort=-pcpu | head -5: if zpa-connector-child is not at the top and another process consumes the CPU, the problem might not be related to the Zscaler service.

quotes: It is important to confirm whether the App Connector process (zpa-connector-child) is truly the cause or whether system-level factors or other applications are contributing.
ps aux --sort=-pcpu | head -5
Validate if zpa-connector-child is at the top.
If another process is consuming CPU, the problem might not be related to the Zscaler service.
evidence.after: Check if the Connector-Child is Running High

cpu-multicore.statement: Top can show CPU utilization above 100% on a multi-core host; the runbook's example is 4 cores with top showing 200%, which means 50%, and lscpu gives the number of cores.

quotes: if the CPU utilization is more than 100%, it might be due to multiple CPU cores on the App Connector host
if there are 4 cores, and the top output is showing CPU utilization as 200%, it means CPU utilization is at 50%.
Use the lscpu command to check the number of cores that the App Connector is running on.

cpu-support-threshold.statement: When CPU utilization is consistently high (more than 80% normalized CPU) over a sustained period and affects users, the runbook says to collect the data listed under "Collecting Logs from the App Connector" and raise a Zscaler Support case; that list shows vmstat output and the memory information read from curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/status and curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/argo.

quotes: In cases where the CPU Utilization is consistently high (i.e., consumes >80% normalized CPU) over a sustained period and is affecting the performance for users, collect the following data and raise a Zscaler Support case.
vmstat Output
curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/status
curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/argo
evidence.after: Memory info on the App Connector for the App Connector processes:

local-memory-endpoints.statement: Memory information for the App Connector processes is read on the host with curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/status and curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/argo.

quotes: curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/status
curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/argo
evidence.after: Memory info on the App Connector for the App Connector processes:

meminfo.statement: When memory is reported high on the Private Access Health dashboard or an alert fires for high memory utilization, the runbook runs cat /proc/meminfo, and treats a larger gap between MemTotal and MemAvailable (relative to total RAM) as possible memory pressure.

quotes: If the memory usage is reported high on the Private Access Health dashboard, or if an alert is generated for high memory utilization, run the /proc/meminfo command to capture more granular memory statistics.
cat /proc/meminfo
A larger gap between MemTotal and MemAvailable (relative to total RAM) might indicate memory pressure.

memory-by-process.statement: To find which process uses memory the runbook runs ps aux --sort=-pmem | head -5 and checks for third-party processes; in its example omiagent uses 84.7% of memory.

quotes: ps aux --sort=-pmem | head -5
validate if there is any third-party processes consuming the system memory
In this example, omiagent is consuming 84.7% of memory, making it the leading potential contributor to high memory utilization.

memory-remedies.statement: To reduce memory use on a connector host the runbook lists increasing host memory, deploying more App Connectors into the group, and deploying dedicated App Connector Groups for specific application segments; if these do not help, collect the memory utilization output (the runbook lists lscpu, ps aux --sort=-pmem, curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/status, curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/arg and sudo journalctl > dump-of-journalctl.txt) and raise a Support case.

quotes: Increase the amount of available memory on the App Connector host.
Deploy additional App Connectors into the App Connector Group to distribute users across additional App Connectors.
Deploy dedicated App Connector Groups for specific application segments to reduce the number of applications that are requested through each App Connector Group.
If none of the earlier steps doesn't help resolve the issue
collect the memory utilization output and raise a case with Zscaler Support.
lscpu ps aux --sort=-pmem curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/status curl -s 127.0.0.1:9000/memory/arg sudo journalctl > dump-of-journalctl.txt

disk-impact-and-floor.statement: Disk utilization issues can make App Connectors throw errors, fail upgrades or hit logging failures; the runbook says to keep at least 100 MB free (otherwise the App Connector might automatically restart) and to treat Use% near 100% on critical filesystems such as / or /var as a risk of disk exhaustion.

quotes: Disk utilization issues can cause Private Access App Connectors to throw errors, fail upgrades, or encounter logging failures.
Ensure at least 100 MB of free disk space is available; otherwise, the App Connector might automatically restart.
If the Use% is close to 100% for critical filesystems (e.g., / or /var), there is a risk of disk exhaustion.

disk-cleanup.statement: For disk cleanup the runbook uses sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=1G to clear space in /var/log/journal, prevents Zscaler processes from using syslogd (journald already stores their logs) and restarts rsyslogd, and, because other processes on the Linux box can still log and use disk space, gives a daily logrotate configuration keeping 7 backlogs in /etc/logrotate.conf as an example.

quotes: Log files, particularly in /var/log, are a frequent cause of high disk utilization.
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=1G clear sspace in /var/log/journal.
Prevent Zscaler processes from using syslogd. journald already stores the logs from Zscaler processes using the following configuration.
systemctl restart rsyslogd
Even if you prevent Zscaler from using syslog, there can be other processes in the Linux box doing the logging and utilizing the disk space.
Here is an example configuration to rotate logs daily.
This configuration needs to be in /etc/logrotate.conf
keep 7 daily worth of backlogs rotate 7

memory-threshold.title: What MemTotal to MemAvailable gap counts as memory pressure, and how long CPU must stay above 80%
memory-threshold.detail: The runbook says only a larger gap between MemTotal and MemAvailable relative to total RAM might indicate memory pressure, with no number. The CPU support threshold is more than 80% normalized CPU over a sustained period, with no duration.
